items.stem: Which of the following best describes "file management"?
options: The ability of an OS to run several processes apparently at the same time by rapidly switching the CPU between them
An algorithm in which the ready process with the highest priority runs next
The OS function that organises files in directories, controls access permissions and maps files to storage blocks
The OS activity of deciding which process in the ready queue gets the CPU and for how long
items.answer: The OS function that organises files in directories, controls access permissions and maps files to storage blocks
items.markingKey: C. "file management" is the OS function that organises files in directories, controls access permissions and maps files to storage blocks.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the user interface and the kernel.
items.answer: The kernel is the privileged core that manages resources; the user interface (GUI or CLI) is the part users interact with to give commands.
items.markingKey: The kernel is the privileged core that manages resources; the user interface (GUI or CLI) is the part users interact with to give commands. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Each program must contain its own code to drive the printer." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Programs send requests to the OS, which uses the printer's device driver; applications do not drive hardware directly.
items.markingKey: Programs send requests to the OS, which uses the printer's device driver; applications do not drive hardware directly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A system uses paging with a page size of 1024 bytes. A process's page table is: page 0 → frame 15, page 1 → frame 8, page 2 → frame 12, page 3 → frame 22, page 4 → frame 20. Translate the logical address 4686 into a physical address.
Identify the operating system function responsible for each task: handling a keyboard interrupt; swapping an inactive page to disk; tracking which disk blocks belong to a file.
items.answer: handling a keyboard interrupt – device management / interrupt handling; swapping an inactive page to disk – memory management; tracking which disk blocks belong to a file – file management
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: handling a keyboard interrupt – device management / interrupt handling; swapping an inactive page to disk – memory management; tracking which disk blocks belong to a file – file management.

items.stem:
(a) Chloé writes: "Paging requires each process to be stored in one continuous block of RAM." Explain why this is inaccurate. [2]
(b) A system uses paging with a page size of 4096 bytes. A process's page table is: page 0 → frame 27, page 1 → frame 15, page 2 → frame 11, page 3 → frame 28, page 4 → frame 3, page 5 → frame 26, page 6 → frame 24. Translate the logical address 1637 into a physical address. [3]
(c) A smartphone runs a music app, a navigation app and a messaging app at once. Describe how the operating system's process management, memory management and device management functions allow this. [6]
items.answer: (a) Paging allows pages to be placed in any free frames, so a process can be scattered across memory. (b) 112229 (c) Process management: each app is a process; the scheduler shares CPU time (time slices, priorities, background vs foreground). Memory: each process gets its own protected address space; paging/virtual memory and suspending background apps free RAM. Devices: drivers give shared access to speaker, GPS and network; the OS arbitrates (e.g. audio focus) and handles interrupts from each device.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Paging allows pages to be placed in any free frames, so a process can be scattered across memory. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (b) [3 marks] Page = 1637 DIV 4096 = 0 (M1); offset = 1637 MOD 4096 = 1637 (M1); frame 27 → physical = 27 × 4096 + 1637 = 112229 (A1). (c) [6 marks] Process management: each app is a process; the scheduler shares CPU time (time slices, priorities, background vs foreground). Memory: each process gets its own protected address space; paging/virtual memory and suspending background apps free RAM. Devices: drivers give shared access to speaker, GPS and network; the OS arbitrates (e.g. audio focus) and handles interrupts from each device.

items.stem: Explain why round robin is suitable for interactive, time-sharing systems.
items.answer: Each process gets the CPU regularly for a short quantum, so no user waits long for a response, giving fair and responsive service even with long jobs present.

items.stem: Three jobs arrive at time 0 in the order J1, J2, J3 with burst times 7, 11 and 6 ms. Calculate the average waiting time under FCFS and under shortest job first, and explain the difference.
items.answer: FCFS 8.33 ms, SJF 6.33 ms; SJF is lower because short jobs no longer wait behind long ones
items.markingKey: FCFS average 8.33 (A1), SJF average 6.33 (A1), explanation that running shorter jobs first reduces the total waiting of the others (R1).

items.stem: A hospital server runs real-time patient-monitoring alerts, interactive staff queries and overnight report generation. Recommend a scheduling strategy, justifying how it handles each type of process and how starvation is avoided.
items.answer: Multilevel (feedback) queue: highest-priority queue for real-time alerts (preemptive priority), middle queue for interactive queries (round robin with short quantum for responsiveness), lowest for batch reports (FCFS/long quantum). Ageing promotes long-waiting batch jobs so they are not starved; reports scheduled overnight when load is low.
items.markingKey: Multilevel (feedback) queue: highest-priority queue for real-time alerts (preemptive priority), middle queue for interactive queries (round robin with short quantum for responsiveness), lowest for batch reports (FCFS/long quantum). Ageing promotes long-waiting batch jobs so they are not starved; reports scheduled overnight when load is low.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Round robin is the best scheduling algorithm for all operating systems."
items.answer: Good for time-sharing, but real systems combine it with priorities (multilevel feedback queues).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fair, no starvation, good response time for interactive users. Arguments against: context-switch overhead; ignores priorities – unsuitable for real-time tasks; higher average turnaround than SJF for batch work. Supported judgement: Good for time-sharing, but real systems combine it with priorities (multilevel feedback queues). Markbands (6 marks): top band: well-balanced discussion with accurate, specific technical detail applied to the context and a justified conclusion; middle band: some balance and correct terminology, conclusion only partly supported; bottom band: descriptive, largely one-sided, little technical detail or application.

items.stem: Explain why multilevel queue scheduling is used in modern operating systems.
items.answer: Different processes have different needs: system and interactive tasks need fast response (high priority, RR), batch jobs need throughput (lower priority, FCFS); separate queues let the OS apply the right policy to each class.

(2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "interrupt".
items.answer: A signal from hardware or software to the CPU that an event needs immediate attention, causing the current task to be suspended

items.stem: Explain the difference between interrupts and polling.
items.answer: With polling the CPU repeatedly checks devices whether or not they need attention (wasting cycles); with interrupts the device signals the CPU only when it needs attention, so the CPU can do other work.
items.markingKey: With polling the CPU repeatedly checks devices whether or not they need attention (wasting cycles); with interrupts the device signals the CPU only when it needs attention, so the CPU can do other work. Interrupts are prioritised (1 = highest) and a higher-priority interrupt pre-empts a running ISR of lower priority. The CPU is idle when these occur: at t = 0 ms a "power failure" interrupt (priority 1, ISR takes 3 ms); at t = 1 ms a "disk read complete" interrupt (priority 2, ISR takes 2 ms); at t = 4 ms a "network packet" interrupt (priority 3, ISR takes 5 ms). State the order in which the ISRs finish and the time each finishes.
items.answer: power failure at 3 ms, disk read complete at 5 ms, network packet at 10 ms
items.markingKey: Order and finishing times: power failure at 3 ms, disk read complete at 5 ms, network packet at 10 ms. 1 mark for the correct order, 1-2 marks for the times; pre-empted ISRs resume after higher-priority ones complete.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Interrupts should be used for every input device."
items.answer: Interrupts suit most infrequent inputs, but high-rate or timing-critical devices may be better served by polling or DMA.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: CPU does useful work instead of checking idle devices; fast response to rare events. Arguments against: each interrupt has overhead for saving/restoring state; very frequent events (high-speed data) can overwhelm the CPU (interrupt storm) – DMA or polling may be better; polling gives deterministic timing. Supported judgement: Interrupts suit most infrequent inputs, but high-rate or timing-critical devices may be better served by polling or DMA.

items.stem: A smart thermostat must read a temperature sensor, respond to the user pressing buttons and receive commands from a phone app over Wi-Fi. For each input, recommend polling or interrupts and justify; then describe what happens when the button interrupt arrives while the CPU is processing a Wi-Fi command.
items.answer: Sensor: polling at a fixed interval (regular, predictable). Buttons: interrupt (rare, needs quick response). Wi-Fi: interrupt when a packet arrives. When the button interrupt arrives: CPU completes the current instruction, checks priority; if higher than the current ISR it saves PC/registers, runs the button ISR, restores state and resumes the Wi-Fi handling; otherwise it is queued until the current ISR finishes.
items.markingKey: Sensor: polling at a fixed interval (regular, predictable). Buttons: interrupt (rare, needs quick response). Wi-Fi: interrupt when a packet arrives. When the button interrupt arrives: CPU completes the current instruction, checks priority; if higher than the current ISR it saves PC/registers, runs the button ISR, restores state and resumes the Wi-Fi handling; otherwise it is queued until the current ISR finishes.

items.stem: Distinguish between starvation and deadlock.
items.answer: In deadlock a set of processes all wait on each other in a cycle and none can ever proceed; in starvation a process waits indefinitely because others keep being chosen, though the system as a whole progresses.

items.stem: For a car's anti-lock braking system, identify suitable sensor(s) and actuator(s), and describe how feedback is used to control it.

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between open-loop control and closed-loop control. [2]
(b) For an automatic door, identify suitable sensor(s) and actuator(s), and describe how feedback is used to control it. [4]
(c) Design an automatic control system for an ICU incubator that keeps a baby's environment at 36.5 °C and 60% humidity. Identify the sensors, actuators and processing, describe the feedback loop, and explain two safety features. [6]
items.answer: (a) Open-loop control acts without measuring the result (e.g. timed sprinkler); closed-loop control measures the output with sensors and feeds it back to correct deviations from the set point. (b) Sensors: infrared/motion sensor. Actuators: electric motor that slides the door. Feedback: the processor repeatedly reads the sensors (via an ADC), compares the values with set points and signals the actuators to correct any difference; the new readings show the effect. (c) Sensors: temperature, humidity (and possibly skin temperature); ADCs convert readings. Processor compares readings with set points every second. Actuators: heater, humidifier, fan; alarm. Loop: read → compare → adjust heater/humidifier → repeat (negative feedback, hysteresis). Safety: redundant sensors and range checks; alarm and fail-safe shutdown if readings are out of range or a sensor fails; manual override.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a thermostat uses a small band (hysteresis) around the set point.
items.answer: If the heater switched exactly at the set point it would turn on and off very rapidly due to noise and small fluctuations, wearing out the relay; a band (e.g. on below 20 °C, off above 22 °C) prevents this.

items.stem: Explain why an operating system is needed between application programs and the hardware.
items.answer: It hides hardware details behind standard services (system calls, drivers), shares the CPU, memory and devices between programs safely, and protects programs from each other, so applications do not need to manage hardware themselves.

items.stem: Explain why interrupts are more efficient than polling for a keyboard.
items.answer: Key presses are infrequent and unpredictable; with polling the CPU wastes cycles checking when nothing has happened, while with interrupts the CPU does other work and only responds when a key is actually pressed.

items.answer: (a) With polling the CPU repeatedly checks devices whether or not they need attention (wasting cycles); with interrupts the device signals the CPU only when it needs attention, so the CPU can do other work. (b) The saved PC and registers are restored so the program resumes exactly where it stopped. (c) Sensor: polling at a fixed interval (regular, predictable). Buttons: interrupt (rare, needs quick response). Wi-Fi: interrupt when a packet arrives. When the button interrupt arrives: CPU completes the current instruction, checks priority; if higher than the current ISR it saves PC/registers, runs the button ISR, restores state and resumes the Wi-Fi handling; otherwise it is queued until the current ISR finishes.

(c) [6 marks] Sensor: polling at a fixed interval (regular, predictable). Buttons: interrupt (rare, needs quick response). Wi-Fi: interrupt when a packet arrives. When the button interrupt arrives: CPU completes the current instruction, checks priority; if higher than the current ISR it saves PC/registers, runs the button ISR, restores state and resumes the Wi-Fi handling; otherwise it is queued until the current ISR finishes.

items.stem: Two print jobs each need the printer (R1) and a scanner (R2). Job A holds R1 and requests R2; job B holds R2 and requests R1. Explain why this is a deadlock with reference to the four necessary conditions, and describe two different ways the OS could prevent or recover from it.
items.answer: Mutual exclusion (devices non-shareable), hold and wait (each holds one, wants another), no preemption (cannot take a device away mid-job), circular wait (A→R2→B→R1→A). Prevention: request both devices at once, or order resources so all jobs request R1 before R2. Recovery: abort one job or preempt its device and roll it back.

items.stem:
Case study context: Sakura Rail, a regional train operator in Osaka, runs real-time signalling on embedded systems, sells tickets online and must protect its network from attacks.
(a) A student claims: "Closed-loop systems keep the output exactly at the set point at all times." Identify the error in this claim and correct it. Refer to Sakura Rail in your answer. [2]
(b) "Computer-controlled systems are safer than human-controlled ones." To what extent do you agree with this statement? Refer to Sakura Rail in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) They correct deviations after they are measured, so the output fluctuates around the set point. (b) Often safer for routine, well-defined tasks, but human oversight and fail-safes remain essential.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] They correct deviations after they are measured, so the output fluctuates around the set point. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: respond faster and consistently, never tired; continuous monitoring with precise sensors. Arguments against: sensor failure or software bugs can cause dangerous behaviour; cannot handle unexpected situations outside their design; vulnerable to cyberattack if networked. Supported judgement: Often safer for routine, well-defined tasks, but human oversight and fail-safes remain essential.
